cells.tense: Right now you are at the point where the pattern bottoms out, and this ground holds.
cells.act: let the feeling settle into its own depth
cells.ask: When something lands uneven between people this week, hold off deciding — let what you feel about it go quiet for a day, then look at the actual proportion.
cells.core:
In what sits between people, you can see the whole shape of a thing without needing to move it. You have gone far enough into your own thinking that you know when a small unevenness is real and when it will right itself, and you can hold it without a verdict. That is this ground working well: fairness arriving out of quiet rather than force, nobody scolded for the simple fact of a feeling.

Let the feeling about the next uneven thing go quiet before you touch it. Not the fact of what happened — the feeling around it. Give it a day of no deciding, then look at what is actually out of proportion. What the heart already knows tends to land before the reasoning catches up, and a call made after that settling holds longer than one made inside the heat. You end up with a verdict you don't have to defend.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel a thing fully and name it fair.
cells.verb: going so deep into the pattern that thinking reaches its own floor
cells.place: where what's out of proportion between people gets set back level

cells.tense: You are bracing to declare how things should stand between people, before they have said what they want.
cells.act: put the frame on the table before anyone asks
cells.ask: Next time a thing between two people is out of joint, say once, plainly, what you think the fair arrangement is — then stop, with no argument after it.
cells.core:
Among people, you are trying to settle the proportions before the ones they concern get a word. The arrangement is clear in your head, the logic is sound, and it arrives before anyone gets asked what they think is fair. From outside it reads as a ruling, and people start managing around it rather than inside it. What you can actually see — patterns that are real, imbalances that matter — gets buried under how it lands. You end up holding a structure nobody agreed to stand in.

Say the frame out loud once and then leave it there. State plainly what you think is out of joint and what the fix would be, then let the others respond without you defending the shape of it. The structure is your strength; the timing is what slips. When you put it down and wait, the people it touches can step inside it, and the fair arrangement becomes theirs to keep instead of yours to enforce.
cells.sheetLine: You're fixing what's crooked before anyone agrees it is.

cells.tense: You keep leaving things between people where they fell, as though the imbalance were already handled.
cells.act: celebrate with the others, not after them
cells.ask: Pick one good thing the people near you already marked together and join the marking — say the gladness out loud alongside them instead of after.
cells.core:
Where things between people are uneven, you have stopped stepping in. Not because you can't see it — you see it more clearly than most — but because you no longer treat the imbalance as yours to touch. The fairness sits there unweighed, and the ones nearby carry it. Holding the thought privately has taken the place of a move. The thinking didn't end; it just stopped coming out, and the space where your read used to land is empty.

Go where the joy already is. Find a good thing the people near you are already marking and mark it with them, out loud, at the same time, not after the fact. Being inside the shared moment is what recharges the part of you that weighs proportion; the read comes back later, once you have stopped standing outside. The fairness follows the belonging. Join in first, then see what is out of balance.
cells.sheetLine: You see what's uneven and you've stopped saying so.

cells.tense: You are already keeping things level among the people near you, and you would call it staying out of it.
cells.act: rest in the connection without doing anything with it
cells.ask: For one gathering with the people near you, do none of the smoothing — no word placed, no weight shifted — and just stay with them.
cells.core:
Where things between people get set right, the setting right is being done. A word here, a slight shift of weight there, and the proportions come back level — and if asked, you would say you had nothing to do with it, that you keep to yourself. The quiet adjustments are not being claimed even by the one making them, so they don't get to count as yours. This ground keeps working, kept by someone who won't put down a name.

One gathering, change nothing. Let a thing between people run its natural length while you stay put in it, without placing the smoothing word or shifting the weight. Watch what actually holds the balance — that is usually the part you do without noticing, and it is easier to see when you stop doing it than when you are doing it. The next time you set something right, you will know it was you.
cells.sheetLine: The balance is kept — by you, without your name on it.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: that this person sets fairness between people from behind the scenes, adjusting without being seen — the record shows the seat, not their history, and nothing licenses a scene. A reader could reasonably say they are simply private, not a hidden keeper, so any example of a dispute and how they handled it would be inventing a life. The asks survive that: each is one bounded act that works whether the seat is occupied by a mediator, a bystander, or someone who merely notices imbalance. The sentence that serves the writer is the Unacknowledged core's 'the people being kept level have not believed it once' — it flatters the read; I removed it and left the two-sided reverie instead.
